CausalChain: High survivin expression in HCC -> Reduced apoptotic cell death and enhanced tumor survival -> Loss of immunogenic signals and establishment of an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment -> CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockdown of survivin (via targeted nanoparticle delivery) -> Induction of apoptotic, immunogenic tumor cell death -> Release of tumor antigens and activation of dendritic cells -> Increased recruitment and activation of CD8+ T cells -> PD-1 blockade further removes T cell inhibition -> Synergistic enhancement of anti-tumor immunity
Hypothesis: Targeted in situ CRISPR/Cas9-mediated suppression of survivin in HCC, delivered using hepatocyte-specific nanoparticle systems and combined with PD-1 immune checkpoint blockade, will synergistically induce immunogenic tumor cell death, enhance T cell infiltration, and overcome the immunosuppressive barrier of HCC, thereby improving therapeutic efficacy.
Abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains a challenging malignancy due to its immunosuppressive microenvironment and resistance to conventional treatments. Recent advances in genome‐editing and immunotherapy have explored targeted interventions based on intrinsic tumor drivers. In this context, we propose that the targeted in situ suppression of survivin – a key anti‐apoptotic protein frequently overexpressed in HCC – via CRISPR/Cas9, when delivered using hepatocyte‐specific nanoparticles, can trigger immunogenic cell death and tumor antigen release. This would lead to enhanced dendritic cell activation and T cell infiltration. When combined with PD-1 immune checkpoint blockade to relieve T cell inhibition, a synergistic anti-tumor response may be realized, potentially improving overall therapeutic outcomes. This hypothesis integrates gene editing with immune modulation to overcome the challenges of HCC’s resistance mechanisms.
